articles.text: The Superior Court of Alameda County is seeking residents to serve on the Alameda County Civil Grand Jury. The jury’s primary responsibility is to examine and report on the operations of local government agencies and to investigate citizen complaints, acting as the public’s watchdog. As a member of the Civil Grand Jury you would work with 18 other panel members to investigate citizen complaints and examine the operations of local government agencies across Alameda County. This work involves reading and analyzing investigative materials, questioning witnesses, and writing reports. Serving on the Grand Jury is a significant commitment. The jury meets twice a week (Wednesday and Thursday mornings) for a year. Most jurors devote additional time beyond this to their service. Grand jurors are paid $15 a day plus mileage and/or public transportation reimbursement. Applications for the 2026- 2027 term (starting July 1) are due by April 1. articles.text: Born on February 2, 1944 in San Francisco, John Speakman passed away on December 23, 2025, at the age of 81 due to the effects of a stroke. A resident of Alamo, he was the Fire Chief in Piedmont from 1997 to 2010. John served in both the Oakland and Piedmont Fire Departments. After serving 29 years in the Oakland Fire Department, he was appointed Fire Chief of Piedmont in 1997, and served ably until his retirement in 2010, bringing 42 years in the fire service to a close. During his tenure, he provided excellent fire protection and emergency medical services to both the Oakland and Piedmont residents, as well as disaster preparedness, CPR, and first aid classes in conjunction with the cities’ changing needs. John spent his retired years occupied by his love of sailing, golfing, cooking, John Speakman and spending time with his two grandchildren, Keoni and Emiko. John is survived by his son, Matthew; daughter-in-law, Cheryl; and his grandchildren, Keoni and Emiko. He is predeceased by his wife, Susan. At his request, there will be no service.
articles.title: Former Piedmont Fire Chief John Speakman dies at 81

Nominate it to become a City of Piedmont Heritage Tree! https://form.jotform. com/240190478826058 To nominate a tree or group of trees, complete the online nomination form by Friday, March 20. Nominators will be asked to provide a brief description explaining what makes the tree noteworthy, the address or general location, and photos of the tree. The Park Commission will consider nominations based on aesthetic, educational or historical qualities. Any tree located in Piedmont parks or other public spaces is eligible. Trees on private property will not be considered. This year’s Heritage Trees will be announced at the April 9, 2026, Park Commission meeting and recognized at the City’s annual Arbor Day celebration on Thursday, April 23, at Community Hall. Nominators of selected trees will be acknowledged during the Arbor Day program and will receive a limited-edition Piedmont Heritage Tree lapel pin. An interactive map of Piedmont’s Heritage Trees is available on the City’s website. Trees selected this year will join 34 others designated since the program began in 2018. piedmont.ca.gov/ HeritageTrees. With questions about the Heritage Tree program, contact Parks & Project Manager Nancy Kent at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: This year, the City is reviving the Volunteer of the Year award for the first time since 2019. The City is also introducing a new award: Young Volunteer of the Year (under age 25), intended to uplift the meaningful contributions young people make across Piedmont. Piedmont has long been known as the “City of Volunteers.” This award, first introduced in 2014, recognizes community members whose volunteer service helped strengthen Piedmont in 2025 – whether through neighborhood improvement, arts and culture, direct community support, or building a more welcoming and inclusive community. Nominations open through March 13 To nominate a volunteer, complete the online nomination form by Friday, March 13: https://form. jotform.com/260417487348162. Volunteer service can take many forms – from a long-running commitment to a concentrated effort that made a real difference in a single year. Nominations may recognize service that strengthened Piedmont through areas such as: • Community enrichment: improving neighborhoods and shared spaces, from beautification and clean-ups to public safety and neighborhood initiatives • Culture & Heritage: preserving local history, celebrating Piedmont’s diverse community, and supporting cultural events • Arts: strengthening the community through the visual and performing arts, arts educa- • • tion, events, and mentorship Social: direct community support and humanitarian service, including work with seniors, children, individuals with disabilities, families, and community health and safety Allyship: fostering belonging and solidarity, challenging bias, and helping make Piedmont a safe and welcoming community for everyone Nominations will be reviewed using a blind scoring process that considers measurable impact, service dedication, innovation and leadership, and character and values. Top-scoring nominees are then forwarded to a City Council subcommittee for final selection. Awardees will be recognized at the City’s annual Volunteer Appreciation Reception on April 20, 2026. articles.text: Piedmont Asian American Club is hosting a Lunar New Year celebration this Friday, February 27, at the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse, providing an evening of performances, food, and community celebration. The annual event will run from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. and feature performances by Piedmont High School students, crafts, a raffle, and a traditional Lion dance. Food and drink will include dim sum, boba drinks, and panang curry. Gourmet desserts and specialty drinks will be provided by Bakesum and Tea on Piedmont. “I encourage all to recognize the contributions of the Asian American community to the community of Piedmont,” said Mayor Betsy Andersen. PAAC representatives Jean Takezawa and Cassindy Chao spoke at the February 17 council meeting, thanking the council for their support of the event. “This proclamation matters, representation matters, public recognition matters. When a city names and honors a community’s tradition, it signals belonging and tells our children that their cultures are not peripheral; they are part of the civic fabric of this place. Thank you for honoring this holiday,” said Takezawa, the Director of Diversity, Equity, Inclusion & Belonging, at PHS Affinity Mentorship Program. PAAC’s Lunar New Year Celebration is open to all community members. “I wanted to invite everybody again to our Lunar New Year event,” said Chao. “What’s nice is that it brings young and old together, and it really shares our community and our culture with everybody.” Tickets are limited and expected to sell out. General admission is $25 and includes dinner. Tickets can be purchased at https://bit.ly/4rlmA6K or by scanning the QR code in the poster. articles.text: Piedmont Unified School District (PUSD) Superintendent Jennifer Hawn will host a community meeting on Thursday, February 26, at 4:30 p.m. in the District Office Board Room, 760 Magnolia Avenue. to discuss sportsmanship and spectator conduct following the January 30 varsity boys basketball game that ended in violent altercations. Community members are invited to attend and participate as the district reviews what occurred following the game between Piedmont and San Leandro High. Hawn will present PUSD’s current conduct rules and recent actions. Time will be reserved at the end for community input. Hawn indicated that this is an important conversation and that sportsmanship must extend beyond the players on the court to include fan behavior. “The energy of our student sections can be one of the most joyful parts of high school athletics, but we also recognize that we have important work to do in developing consistently positive approaches to student fan behavior. School spirit should encourage our team while showing respect for opponents, officials, and visiting families,” Hawn wrote in her Piedmont Pulse newsletter on February 9. It is available at Smore.com/n/tu493. As a result of the fight in the PHS gym, Piedmont’s basketball team played without fans in attendance on February 4. In his February 13 Parent Newsletter, PHS Principal David Yoshihara shared his hopes of turning the page on the regrettable incident. “Three of our teams should make playoffs, which start next week,” Yoshihara said. “Feel free to come support our Highlanders if you’re in town and want to help us farm aura in the gym or on the field. It should be a lot of fun ... emphasizing FUN.” Hawn’s meeting is not the first action taken by district leadership. Yoshihara also led a discussion about the January 30 boys basketball game and its aftermath during the PHS Parents’ Club morning meeting on Friday, February 13. In her most recent Piedmont Pulse newsletter, Hawn applauded the role model efforts that were made that night in the face of the chaotic scene. “Thank you to Ben Spencer, Shamaree Worley, all of our basketball coaches, David Yoshihara, and especially Tyler Small for their remarkable leadership and steady presence in keeping our players and students safe during Friday night’s basketball game. Their professionalism and care reflect the very best of our district,” she said. “However, district staff shall not obstruct, interfere with, or otherwise impede an officer or employee of an agency conducting immigration enforcement who nonetheless enters district-provided transportation, a nonpublic area of any district property or facility, or a nonpublic area where any district-sponsored program or activity is occurring.” PUSD’s policy also requires the Superintendent, or a designee, to report to the Board in a timely manner any requests by an officer or employee of an agency conducting immigration enforcement. The requirement is in effect if the requests are about: a student or their household’s information, personnel records of employee, or permission to enter district provided transportation, and district non-public areas. articles.text: Piedmont High’s Advanced Acting class will present the acclaimed play Eurydice, by Sarah Ruhl, in the Alan Harvey Theater on Friday and Saturday, March 6-7 at 7:00 p.m. each night. Eurydice is a comedic drama that reimagines the classic myth of Orpheus and Eurydice, focusing on Eurydice’s journey through the Underworld. Reunited with her deceased Mother, Eurydice must grapple with forgotten memories of her past life while facing a life-altering choice. With contemporary characters and plot twists, Eurydice is a fresh look at love and loss. The play is directed by senior Amelia Addington with a cast that includes Yiyou Fang, Kirstin Fedor, Jack Herrlinger, Nico Kaltenecker, Sparrow Lieu, Lila Schwab, and Grette Willats. Addington said she is excited to direct the show because of its creative and poetic natures. “Its abstract storytelling and emotional depth allow both the cast and the audience to interpret the story in different and personal ways,” she said. With nearly 20 plays and a MacArthur Genius Grant to her name, author Sarah Ruhl is one of the most important American playwrights of our time. The Advanced Acting Class has previously produced her shows, Dead Man’s Cell Phone and The Clean House. Eurydice has been produced from high schools to Broadway, and it has been translated into 14 languages. In 2021, Ruhl adapted Eurydice into an opera that was performed during the New York Metropolitan Opera season. Eurydice is recommended for most audiences, though some material may not be suitable for younger audience members. This production explores themes of love, loss, memory, and the afterlife. For more information contact producer Kimberly Taylor at ktaylor@piedmont.k12.ca.us. Tickets are $5 for students and $10 for general admission. Tickets may be purchased at phsacting. ludus.com or with cash at the door.

articles.text: Piedmont for Inclusive Education (PIE) will host its second annual benefit concert supporting the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Sidekicks program on February 27. The concert will feature We Are Leaves, formerly The Date Nights, a band made up of Piedmont parents, at Piedmont Community Hall from 7 to 9 p.m. The band, consisting of Beach Elementary parents, describes its music as “indie pop.” Lead singer and guitarist Matthew Zapruder said the group writes “songs that have recognizable melodies and structures but are maybe a little quirkier than those you might hear in your car on the radio.” “We write songs about our local community: they mention Dracena Park and its audible owls, as well as a local ghost who lives in Dracena named Celeste,” said Zapruder. Proceeds from the concert will benefit the Sidekicks program, led by Larisa Martiniak. The program pairs neurodiverse children with a dedicated teen sidekick to help them navigate activities, build social connections and participate more fully and confidently in summer camps and other programs. Through the experience, teen sidekicks develop communication skills, patience, adaptability and emotional intelligence. Photo by Sasha Przybyla We Are Leaves will play live music at the Sidekicks Benefit Concert, with Matthew Zapruder (left) (lead vocals and guitar), Peter Jaeschke (bass), and Supina Mapon (violin and vocals). Steve Pearson (drums) and Miles Boison (guitar) not pictured. “Having older kids help neurodivergent kids in after-school and other programs makes inclusion actually happen, by supporting families and kids who wouldn’t otherwise be able to participate in those activities,” said Zapruder. The Sidekicks program trains Piedmont teens to support safe, fun and inclusive after-school classes and summer programs for neurodiverse school-aged children. Last year, Sidekicks supported more than 60 Piedmont participants, and 45 teen sidekicks were trained. “The Sidekicks program has changed my kid’s life. He has so much more confidence having a buddy help him through what could easily be overwhelming experiences,” said one Piedmont parent. Sidekicks program offerings, new classes and camps, and increased staff training will be supported by the concert. Learn more about the Sidekicks program at Piedmont. ca.gov/services___departments/ recreation/adaptive_programs__ sidekicks. pages.text: Wednesday, February 25, 2026 7 Advanced Acting Class to stage Eurydice on March 6 & 7 By Kimberly Taylor Piedmont High’s Advanced Acting class will present the acclaimed play Eurydice, by Sarah Ruhl, in the Alan Harvey Theater on Friday and Saturday, March 6-7 at 7:00 p.m. each night. Eurydice is a comedic drama that reimagines the classic myth of Orpheus and Eurydice, focusing on Eurydice’s journey through the Underworld. Reunited with her deceased Mother, Eurydice must grapple with forgotten memories of her past life while facing a life-altering choice. With contemporary characters and plot twists, Eurydice is a fresh look at love and loss. The play is directed by senior Amelia Addington with a cast that includes Yiyou Fang, Kirstin Fedor, Jack Herrlinger, Nico Kaltenecker, Sparrow Lieu, Lila Schwab, and Grette Willats. Addington said she is excited to direct the show because of its creative and poetic natures. “Its abstract storytelling and emotional depth allow both the cast and the audience to interpret the story in different and personal ways,” she said. With nearly 20 plays and a MacArthur Genius Grant to her name, author Sarah Ruhl is one of the most important American playwrights of our time. The Advanced Acting Class has previously produced her shows, Dead Man’s Cell Phone and The Clean House. Eurydice has been produced from high schools to Broadway, and it has been translated into 14 languages. In 2021, Ruhl adapted Eurydice into an opera that was performed during the New York Metropolitan Opera season. Eurydice is recommended for most audiences, though some material may not be suitable for younger audience members. This production explores themes of love, loss, memory, and the afterlife. For more information contact producer Kimberly Taylor at ktaylor@piedmont.k12.ca.us. Tickets are $5 for students and $10 for general admission. Tickets may be purchased at phsacting. ludus.com or with cash at the door. The concert will feature We Are Leaves, formerly The Date Nights, a band made up of Piedmont parents, at Piedmont Community Hall from 7 to 9 p.m. The band, consisting of Beach Elementary parents, describes its music as “indie pop.” Lead singer and guitarist Matthew Zapruder said the group writes “songs that have recognizable melodies and structures but are maybe a little quirkier than those you might hear in your car on the radio.” “We write songs about our local community: they mention Dracena Park and its audible owls, as well as a local ghost who lives in Dracena named Celeste,” said Zapruder. Proceeds from the concert will benefit the Sidekicks program, led by Larisa Martiniak. The program pairs neurodiverse children with a dedicated teen sidekick to help them navigate activities, build social connections and participate more fully and confidently in summer camps and other programs. Through the experience, teen sidekicks develop communication skills, patience, adaptability and emotional intelligence. Photo by Sasha Przybyla We Are Leaves will play live music at the Sidekicks Benefit Concert, with Matthew Zapruder (left) (lead vocals and guitar), Peter Jaeschke (bass), and Supina Mapon (violin and vocals). Steve Pearson (drums) and Miles Boison (guitar) not pictured. “Having older kids help neurodivergent kids in after-school and other programs makes inclusion actually happen, by supporting families and kids who wouldn’t otherwise be able to participate in those activities,” said Zapruder. The Sidekicks program trains Piedmont teens to support safe, fun and inclusive after-school classes and summer programs for neurodiverse school-aged children. Last year, Sidekicks supported more than 60 Piedmont participants, and 45 teen sidekicks were trained. “The Sidekicks program has changed my kid’s life. He has so much more confidence having a buddy help him through what could easily be overwhelming experiences,” said one Piedmont parent. Sidekicks program offerings, new classes and camps, and increased staff training will be supported by the concert. articles.text: In spring, Piedmont Council’s five troops (youth groups for all kids, boys and girls, in 5th grade and up) open their doors to families interested in the scouting program. Open house meetings are an opportunity for kids and their parents to visit a specific scout troop, meet youth and adult leadership, and learn about that troop’s unique brand of scouting. Troops also share highlights from recent campouts, and discuss upcoming activities. Scouting is a time-honored tradition in the community of Piedmont, with 20% of Piedmont youth involved in the program. Scouting provides youth with hands-on leadership experiences and allows them to practice life skills while serving their community. It instills citizenship and character, fosters communication, and builds a self-reliance in youth as they organize events and take on challenges together. He recently returned home to break his own course record at the Piedmont Turkey Trot. It’s amazing to think he once felt overwhelmed setting up a tent on his first Yosemite trip and now leads college friends on backpacking trips to Joshua Tree and the Lost Coast. Our middle son, George, balanced Scouting with water polo throughout high school and discovered something just as powerful as competition: community. He built friendships across age groups while camping and participating in high adventure trips to Sea Base and Northern Tier. Now playing club water polo at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, he continues to enjoy the outdoors along the Central Coast. His journey to team captain began with teaching younger Scouts how to tie knots – skills he later perfected in pursuit of catching the next big fish on trips to Kirby Cove and Dillon Beach. Henry, our youngest, is currently a Life Scout in Troop 11 and a dedicated water polo player. After years of learning alongside his older brothers, he is finishing his Eagle requirements and final merit badges – building confidence, perseverance, and the readiness to step forward and guide others when it counts. Because Scouting is Scoutled, older Scouts teach and guide younger ones—sometimes it’s messy, but that’s where real growth happens. The leadership, resilience, and accountability practiced in Scouts now guide our boys in school, athletics, friendships, and the fields they are pursuing. Just as importantly, they learned how to balance multiple commitments – sports, academics, and service – without giving up one passion for another. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s season came to a close, falling to No. 5 Albany in the NCS Quarterfinals. Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team’s season came to an end on Saturday, February 21, when they were upset by No. 5 Albany, 58-49, at Binks Rawlings Gym. Piedmont was seeded No. 4 in the Division 2 North Coast Section postseason playoffs. It defeated No.13 Urban 55-46 in the opening round at home on Wednesday, February 18. It marks the first time Piedmont hasn’t reached the semifinal round of the NCs playoffs since 2018. “The better team won tonight,” said PHS coach Ben Spencer. “Of our five keys to the game, we didn’t do three of them. It’s the earliest we’ve exited the postseason in seven years, so that feels pretty weird.” Second-chance points and missed opportunities told the story for the Highlanders, getting outrebounded 47-25. Piedmont finished 4-of-25 for 3-pointers and missed nine free throws on the night, including six in a row in the third quarter. “On top of second-chance points, we were miserable cold from the floor. We started 1-for- 13 from three, and missed six free throws in a row in the third quarter. Sometimes that’s just how the night goes, but give credit to Albany. They beat us fair and square,” Spencer said. The result comes as a bit of a surprise after the Highlanders closed its regular season in stellar form with four straight wins over strong opponents – Bishop O’Dowd, Berkeley, Alameda, and Castro Valley. “We were really on a hot streak. There were stretches where I thought we’d get back in the game and figure things out, but it didn’t come to fruition,” Spencer said. “I can’t say I noticed anything bad in practice throughout the week. We just got beat,” mentioned senior captain Dillon Casey. Casey closes his Piedmont High career among the school’s best all-time scorers. He finished No. 4 on the school’s list with 1,392 points behind No. 1 A.J. Harris (1,581), No. 2 Sean Rodriguez (1,541), No. 3 Eric Flato (1,402), and ahead of No. 5 JoJo Murphy (1,355). PHS will see several key players depart with the Class of 2026, including Casey, P.J. Brayer, Akash Bornstein, and Cash Panico. Carrying the torch will be Beach Lorin, who was the team’s second leading scorer behind Casey, and Lucian Fang-Ring. “Beach was killer this year, there’s not much that’s going to stop him next year. We have Lucian, and those two will be the dynamic duo,” Casey said. 58-49 loss to No. 5 Albany Albany led 12-9 through the first quarter, but Piedmont took a lead at the 5:55 mark of the second quarter with five straight points via Casey assisting FangRing for a 3-pointer, while FangRing stole a ball and then assisted Casey for a layup to make it 14-12. However, the Cougars took the lead with a 9-3 run to end the quarter leading 21-16. Albany maintained the fivepoint lead through the midway Dillon Casey finished his Piedmont career No. 4 on the school’s All-Time scoring list with 1,392 points in four years.

articles.text: It was a rough ending for Piedmont High’s girls’ soccer team. The Highlanders, the No. 5 seeded team, traveled to No. 5 Sonoma Academy in Santa Rosa on a cold Saturday, February 21, falling 2-1 in extra time in the North Coast Section Division 2 quarterfinals. To get there, PHS beat No. 12 Acalanes 3-nil at Witter Field on Tuesday, February 17. The result brings Piedmont’s record to 10-2-8 (W-T-L) to end coach Matt Spencer-Harty’s first year at the helm. Their Div. 2 NCS berth marked a two-division jump from last year, when they were the top seed in Div.4. “I’ve enjoyed every minute of it. The girls were great, the personalities were good fun. I’m excited to get it started again because it’s such a great group,” coach Matt Spencer-Harty said. Leaving a sour taste from Saturday’s loss was the way Sonoma Academy scored its opening goal, where a Sonoma striker clearly corralled the ball with the bicep area of her arm before scoring. If the proper call was made, the Highlanders’ could have walked out with a 1-nil victory. “Without a doubt it was a handball. The center referee is 40 yards behind the play, so he couldn’t see it. The linesman is 20 yards back, so he couldn’t see it as well. I asked for an explanation, but they couldn’t explain why. That should’ve ended 1-nil to us, so that was really frustrating,” Spencer-Harty said. Regardless, there is a lot to be proud of from this year’s girls’ soccer team. Spencer-Harty made inroads on an aggressive style in his first year as head coach, while young stars emerged: freshmen Olivia Nealon, Olivia Kan-Miller, Olivia Lucaccini, and Makenna Small, and sophomores Ayla Blanford and Teah Suhr. Looking ahead to next year, the team could have some solid leadership along its back line with Chloe Toyama, Erica Smith, and Daniella Lucaccini as senior defenders. “One person I’d like to highlight is Olivia Nealon,” Spencer-Harty said. “She’s been unbelievable this season. She was probably our best player against Acalanes and she’s only a freshman. We’re losing some important players, but there’s a core group of freshman and sophomores who can step up.” 2-1 loss to Sonoma Academy Sonoma Academy’s goal in the 52nd minute came after a slow pass was played back to PHS goalkeeper Rachel Young. The Coyotes’ forward tried to chip the ball past Young rushing off her line, causing the ball to hit off the Highlanders’ keeper and skip upward. Then, the striker brought the ball down off of her extended arm before slotting in a shot. Young repeatedly signaled to the referee for a handball, but no call was made. Piedmont answered just three minutes later on some terrific interplay and a finish by Miranda Liu for her final goal as a Highlander. It started with Elia Kwong playing a pass to Blanford, who sent a pass back to Kwong on her first touch. Kwong chipped the ball over the defense to Liu Olivia Nealon had two assists against Acalanes. Staff Photos Miranda Liu scored once against Sonoma Academy, and twice against Acalanes in her final two appearances for Piedmont High. charging into the box, leading to Liu wrapping her left foot around the ball on its second bounce. PHS had shots from Nealon and Arden Sorensen-Wald go wide in the 60th, but both teams traded possession for the final 20 minutes of regulation. Five minutes into extra time, Daniella Lucaccini cleared a near goal off the line that led to a Sonoma corner kick, where a defensive header looped the ball toward the right post. A Coyotes’ forward lifted a looping pass to the opposite post, leading to her teammate rising for a header in close distance to score the golden goal. 3-0 shutout of Acalanes Piedmont got its first goal of the game at the 10 minute mark, when Kan-Miller sent in a shot following a corner. It started with Sorensen-Wald sending a cross toward the net, leading to the Dons’ keeper parrying the ball. It fell to Liu, who fired a shot that deflected off a defender. KanMiller was opportunely in position to slot in a shot. After that, a lightning delay stopped play for about an hour. Liu got the second goal in the 31st minute. It started with Blanford playing a pass off the right sideline centrally to Nealon. The freshman took one touch around a charging defender, playing a pass through Acalanes’ back line to Liu in behind. Liu sent a shot from a couple of yards outside the box to the right post for the goal. PHS’ last goal came in the 45th by Liu, once again. This time, Nealon gained possession in the attacking third, rolling a pass to Liu in the box. With her first touch, Liu chipped the ball past the charging Dons’ GK.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Slate.com Alysa Liu of Oakland has risen to star status after winning a gold medal at the Olympics. The 2026 Winter Olympics has officially concluded. The United States finished second place in the medal count with six gold, 10 silver, and five bronze medals. Norway, once again, led the Winter Olympics with 31 medals. Oakland’s Alysa Liu becomes a star 20-year-old Alysa Liu captured Olympic gold in the women’s free skate event, becoming a star in the process. Her gold medal marked a moment of personal triumph for the Bay Area talent, who trains at Oakland Ice Center, after retiring from skating following the 2022 Olympics for her own mental health. It marked Team USA’s first gold medal in the women’s event since 2002. Making the moment even more special for those in the Bay Area was how Liu paid tribute to Oakland, shouting out The Town on multiple occasions, saying she was glad to bring Oakland to Milan. Fenton’s Creamery on Piedmont Ave. declared Liu has “ice cream for life.” Oakland mayor Barbara Lee announced that the city is planning a celebration for Liu. “The City of Oakland is planning a community-wide celebration to honor Olympic gold medalist and Oakland’s hometown hero Alysa Liu! Her achievement has filled our city with pride, and we are coordinating with her team now to finalize a date so the community can celebrate her together,” Lee wrote on Instagram. Team USA women’s hockey edges by Canada in overtime Team USA won the women’s hockey gold medal by defeating rival Canada 2-1 in a thrilling overtime victory on February 19. The Americans went undefeated through the tournament, outscoring opponents 33-2, but struggled to find the same fluidity in the gold medal match. In the game, Canada took a 1-0 lead on a shorthanded goal in the second period, but the U.S. responded late when veteran captain Hilary Knight tipped in a shot with just over two minutes left to tie the score and force overtime. Knight’s goal set new U.S. Olympic records for most career goals. Four minutes into a 3-on-3 sudden-death overtime, Megan Keller scored the golden goal, making a wicked deke by a defender before finishing with a backhand finish into the net. It marked the United States’ third Olympic gold. U.S. men’s hockey stuns Canada Much similarly to the women’s side, Team USA’s men’s hockey team captured an historic gold medal, defeating rival Canada 2-1 in overtime on February 22. It was the U.S.’s first gold medal since the famed “Miracle on Ice” in 1980, ending a 46-year drought. The Americans jumped ahead early with a goal from Matt Boldy in the first period, but Canada responded to tie the game. Goalie Connor Hellebuyck was monumental, stopping 41 of 42 shots. In the 3-on-3 overtime period, Jack Hughes delivered the dramatic golden goal one minute and 41 seconds in, ripping the puck past Canadian goalie Jordan Binnington to seal the victory.

articles.text: Piedmont Council is digging up adventure for its annual Cub Scout Day Camp. Piedmont Cub Scouts and all youth (rising 1st to 5th graders) will be returning to Dracena to journey back in time for camp’s prehistoric “Dinos” theme. During Day Camp, June 15 – 18, campers will take part in a wide range of activities including Scout Skills which showcase the Scouting program. Sports and games will get campers active, arts and crafts will challenge creativity, STEM activities will promote simple scientific thoughts. Day Camp will end on Thursday with its traditional egg drop in partnership with the Piedmont Fire Department. Day Camp is planned by a collaborative team of youth from Piedmont Council’s five Scout BSA troops and Community Service Crew. Those Scouts not only plan the camp activities, but also spend the week as staff, guiding the campers through all the fun things they planned. Coming onboard as 2026’s Program Advisor is Rebecca Fisher, former Pack 5 Cubmaster and current Troop 11 parent. The Council is putting on its archaeological gear and getting ready to run a program full of adventure at Dracena, “The tradition of day camp continues for longtime attendees and new campers alike,” said District Executive Eris Turner. “It brings together youth from across our community for an experience they rarely get and even brings the neighborhood and past Scouts out for the egg drop. It’s truly a special week for everyone involved.” Interested youth can register for Day Camp through the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Community Pass catalog (piedmont.ca.gov/activityguide). articles.text: When we picture summer camp, we tend to imagine the highlights: the lake at sunset, kids on a ropes course, a campfire under the stars. And when we evaluate camps, we usually ask the sensible questions — safety, staff ratios, medical coverage, All are important. But if you talk to teens or adults about what shaped them at camp, they rarely describe the zip line. They describe the counselor who helped them navigate conflict, the tone of the cabin at night, the feeling of belonging, or the way adults responded when something went wrong. Those elements don’t always show up in brochures. They live in the culture. Here are five questions that may gently reveal that culture. 1. What is your philosophy around discipline? Most camps today aren’t punitive. The deeper question is how they understand behavior. When a child struggles — socially, emotionally, or impulsively — is the response primarily corrective, or developmental? In my work around coaching children’s behavior (parCampers at Camp Augusta enjoy a healthy meal around the table with their counselors. entingtuneup.org), discipline is framed as skill-building: emotional regulation, perspective-taking, responsibility, and repair. A camp that thinks this way will speak about growth, coaching, and restoring relationships — not just enforcing rules. You’re listening for how adults guide, not how they correct. 2. What does staff training focus on beyond the required basics? Every camp must cover safety procedures and personnel policies. That’s foundational. But what else fills the training days? Do they prepare counselors to understand child development? Group dynamics? Homesickness? Conflict mediation? Inclusive practices? Emotional coaching? How to notice the quiet child who isn’t asking for help? A detailed schedule may be hard to parse, and what matters is what leaders emphasize. If they speak thoughtfully about belonging, guiding peer relationships, creating community, communication skill building, that tells you something. If you really want to deep dive, ask for some of the lesson plans. Activities are visible. Adult preparation is not — yet it shapes nearly everything your child experiences. 3. In the last decade, how many campers have required emergency services — and for what general reasons? This isn’t about expecting perfection. It’s about transparency and learning. No meaningful residential program operates for years without incidents. What matters is whether the camp tracks patterns, speaks calmly about them, and adapts. articles.text: On a summer morning at Walker Creek Ranch, music brings everyone together before breakfast. Sunlight glimmers through the trees, voices rise from cabins, and campers head outside, greeting each other and the rising sun with song. This is the setting for Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir’s (PEBCC) Summer 2026 sleepaway camps, returning to Marin County this summer. Spread across 1,700 acres of forest, grassland, and trails, Walker Creek Ranch gives young singers a rare chance to step away from screens and school schedules, to spend their days learning, exploring, and making music together. Campers splash at the pond, hike the trails, and discover the beauty of the outdoors. Everyone is accepted for who they are, creating a community where singing and being together are at the heart of each day. PEBCC offers two summer camp experiences. Camp Joyful Voices, a six-day program for singers ages 7 to 11, is designed with younger campers in mind. Days balance rehearsals and musicianship classes with crafts, spirit days, swimming, and games. Colorful friendship bracelets appear on wrists within days, and campers sing on hikes, at mealtimes, and around the campfire. No prior experience is required, so every child can join and experience the joy of singing. Choir Camp, PEBCC’s flagship twelve-day program for singers ages 10 to 15, adds deeper musical focus while keeping the same sense of shared adventure. Campers rehearse daily, study music theory, and participate in vocal lessons, while also hiking to the lake, kayaking, and gathering under the redwood trees for evening songs. articles.text: Shotgun Players will open its 34th season on March 21 with The Goat or, Who is Sylvia? by Edward Albee at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley. The Tony Award-winning play centers on Martin Gray, a successful architect whose personal life unravels after he tells his wife and son that he is in love with a goat named Sylvia. The disclosure leads to conflict within his family and raises questions about morality, loyalty and acceptance. The production is directed by Shotgun Players company member Kevin Clarke. In a statement, Clarke said the play “tests the limits of permissiveness” and asks audiences to consider the characters’ perspectives. William Giammona plays Martin Gray. Erin Mei Ling Stuart portrays his wife, Stevie Gray. Kevin Singer appears as Ross, a longtime family friend, and Joel Ochoa plays the couple’s son, Billy. The play premiered on Broadway in 2002 and won the Tony Award for best play. It was also named a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for drama in 2003. Performances run March 21 through April 19. Showtimes are 7 p.m. Wednesdays and Thursdays, 8 p.m. Fridays and Saturdays, and 2 p.m. Sundays. Preview performances are scheduled for March 21, 22, 25, 26 and 27. Opening night is March 28. A masked matinee is planned for March 29. A haptic tour and live audio-described performance will be offered April 12, with the tour at 1 p.m. and the performance at 2 p.m. Post-show discussions will follow Thursday and Sunday performances. A special event for theatergoers 25 and younger is scheduled for April 2. The Ashby Stage is located at 1901 Ashby Ave. Tickets are available at shotgunplayers.org or by calling 510-841-6500 ext. 303.

articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony ushers in the Year of the Horse with a special Lunar New Year concert held Saturday, February 28. The symphony’s annual Lunar New Year event occurs each February at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco, drawing upon Asian customs and musical heritage to mark one of the most important holidays across East, South and Southeast Asian cultures. This year’s concert is conducted by Mei-Ann Chen, a Taiwanese-American orchestra conductor who has been Music Director of the MacArthur Award-winning Chicago Sinfonietta since 2011. She also serves as Chief Conductor of Austria’s Recreation Grosses Orchester Graz at the Styriarte festival, making her the first female Asian conductor in that role. The symphony is joined by clarinetist Yuhsin Galaxy Su and Erhu player George Gao. An erhu is a traditional Chinese twostringed bowed instrument, often described as a type of spike fiddle, and is one of the most prominent instruments in Chinese classical, folk, opera, and contemporary music. articles.text: San Francisco Ballet presents The Blake Works, a full evening-length exploration of choreographer William Forsythe’s ongoing collaboration with Grammy Award-winning musician James Blake, beginning this Friday, February 27. The program marks the company premiere of Forsythe’s latest works and brings together new material with audience favorites in a first-of-its-kind North American presentation. The Blake Works is a dynamic collection that reimagines ballet through Forsythe’s signature deconstructed aesthetic. Set to Blake’s layered, atmospheric soundscapes, the evening features Prologue, The Barre Project, and Blake Works I. Originally developed during the pandemic, The Barre Project draws inspiration from traditional ballet barre training, transforming foundational exercises into striking performance material. Together, the works form a high-energy, rhythmically charged journey that pushes classical technique into thrilling contemporary territory. The program also reflects a broader movement in ballet, as choreographers continue to explore the expressive possibilities of Blake’s music. At New York City Ballet, choreographer Kyle Abraham has similarly harnessed Blake’s pop sensibility. Building on the momentum of 2018’s The Runaway, Abraham’s Love Letter, his fourth work for the company, features music by Blake and premiered at the 2022 Fall Fashion Gala. The ballet for Photo courtesy of San Francisco Ballet The program highlights choreographer William Forsythe’s ongoing collaboration with Grammy Award-winning musician James Blake. 16 dancers pairs classical virtuosity with contemporary swagger, complemented by bold costumes from British fashion designer Giles Deacon and lighting by Dan Scully. While distinct in style, both Forsythe and Abraham demonstrate how Blake’s evocative sound world can inspire ballet artists to new physical and emotional heights. With The Blake Works, San Francisco Ballet celebrates Forsythe’s enduring innovative spirit and offers audiences a powerful vision of ballet’s future. “As SF Ballet’s repertoire continues to evolve and expand, we invite audiences to experience a season representing the best ballet has to offer, with our worldclass dancers bringing to life a dynamic range of classical and contemporary choreography and stories capturing everything from the drama of the everyday to the mythic and ethereal,” said Tamara Rojo, Artistic Director of SF Ballet. “We will continue to share this spirit of innovation and excellence beyond the Opera House stage as we bring the company across the country and the world.” The Blake Works shows at The War Memorial Opera House this Friday through March 8. Tickets for upcoming performances by San Francisco Ballet are available through the company’s official website, https://www.sf ballet. org. Patrons can purchase single tickets, season packages or buildyour-own series directly online by selecting a performance and clicking the ticket link. Tickets are also available by phone at 415-865-2000, Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. On performance days, the box office at the War Memorial Opera House opens approximately four hours before curtain.

articles.text: Laurence Rupp, Sebastian Urzendowsky, Yoran Leicher, and Leonard Kunz in The Tank trate deep behind Soviet lines and extract a Lieutenant Colonel von Hardenburg from a secret bunker. The colonel has intelligence that could prove catastrophic if it falls into Russian hands. It’s a suicide mission dressed up as a rescue operation. They set off into no man’s land, and things immediately feel wrong. Not in the conventional war-movie sense of escalating danger but wrong in a more fundamental way. The forests are too quiet. The corpses they pass seem oddly decomposed. Time behaves strangely—their watches stopped when they cheated death in the first battle. Encounters with the enemy take on a ritualistic, almost mythological quality. The crew, pumped full of Wehrmacht-issued methamphetamine, can’t trust their own perceptions anymore. Schüt ter’s per for mance anchors the growing unreality. He says it, one suspects, to reassure himself. The phrase becomes a kind of incantation throughout the film, spoken with increasing desperation as the mission deteriorates and reality itself seems to buckle. By the time the credits roll, that simple sentence has been turned inside out and ultimately revealed as the most dangerous lie a soldier can tell himself. The Tank arrives on Prime Video disguised as something audiences already know: a World War II tank thriller in the vein of Brad Pitt’s Fury, complete with claustrophobic interiors, muddy Eastern Front landscapes, and the tension of men sealed inside a metal coffin while death circles outside. Gansel, who directed episodes of Das Boot and made his reputation with Die Welle (The Wave), understands how to wring suspense from confined spaces. When Gerkens’s Tiger tank submerges in a river to hide from Soviet forces, the sequence rivals anything in Wolfgang Petersen’s submarine masterpiece. The premise is straightforward; Autumn 1943, occupied Ukraine. Gerkens and his fiveman crew receive orders to peneLaurence Rupp, Sebastian Urzendowsky, Yoran Leicher, and Leonard Kunz in The Tank trate deep behind Soviet lines and extract a Lieutenant Colonel von Hardenburg from a secret bunker. The colonel has intelligence that could prove catastrophic if it falls into Russian hands. It’s a suicide mission dressed up as a rescue operation. They set off into no man’s land, and things immediately feel wrong. Not in the conventional war-movie sense of escalating danger but wrong in a more fundamental way. The forests are too quiet. The corpses they pass seem oddly decomposed. Time behaves strangely—their watches stopped when they cheated death in the first battle. Encounters with the enemy take on a ritualistic, almost mythological quality. The crew, pumped full of Wehrmacht-issued methamphetamine, can’t trust their own perceptions anymore. Schüt ter’s per for mance anchors the growing unreality. He plays Gerkens as a man who has built his entire identity around the chain of command, around the idea that orders flow downward and responsibility flows upward. It’s a seductive bargain: do what you’re told, and you’re absolved of moral weight. Each time he repeats his mantra – we follow orders – you can see him reinforcing the walls of this prison he’s built for himself. The rest of the cast sketches out alternative responses. Sebastian Urzendowsky’s Keilig, a former teacher, keeps asking “why” even when answers would be dangerous. For a German filmmaker making a World War II movie, there’s no redemptive arc available. American war films can end with victory over evil. But what does a German director do with the Eastern Front, where his grandfather’s generation committed horrors that still echo? Those burning Ukrainian villages in the background aren’t just atmosphere. They’re evidence. The film never lets you forget that these men, sympathetic as they might be individually, are part of an occupying force engaged in a war of annihilation. This is where The Tank becomes genuinely uncomfortable. Gansel forces you to spend two hours inside the heads of Wehrmacht soldiers, to understand their fear and exhaustion, and then refuses to let any of that erase what they’re complicit in. The German press hasn’t quite known what to do with it. Andreas Kilb in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung called it “technically brilliant, but morally problematic,” noting that the victims remain largely invisible. The Süddeutsche Zeitung suggested tank enthusiasts might enjoy it but everyone else should probably stay away. Gansel is asking a question Germans have been asking for eighty years: what do you do with the knowledge that ordinary people, not monsters, just ordinary people following orders, committed extraordinary evil? They’re somewhere much hotter, somewhere final, and the officer who commanded him can offer no protection now, instead of orders come questions. articles.text: Dear Jim I’ve been noticing a lot of issues at my home, such as drainage problems in my basement and crawlspace, more cracks inside on the walls and ceilings that are getting bigger, and I have a sloping floor in my dining room. I have had several contractors out to help me solve these issues, but they all have very different opinions and prices for the work. How can I understand who to hire and the right approach for the work? In the Bay Area, foundation and drainage issues are more than an inconvenience — they threaten your home’s structural integrity. Unfortunately, many homeowners find themselves overwhelmed by a sea of conflicting opinions from contractors. Prioritize Diagnostics Over “Eyeballing” The most important step in any foundation or drainage repair is a thorough inspection. If a contractor provides a bid based solely on a walk-around of your exterior, be cautious. A foundation and drainage specialist should be able to diagnose, design and clearly explain the proposed approach without immediately deferring to a thirdparty engineer or architect who is not on site and may miss critical details. The best specialists bring in engineering support when appropriate, but their field experience in defining the proper scope of work is essential. 3. Decoding the “Different Opinions” When bids vary widely, there are usually important reasons. articles.text: Tucked into the rolling hills of Sonoma County’s Russian River Valley, Dehlinger Winery marks its 50th anniversary this year as one of the region’s most respected and enduring family-owned wine estate. Founded in 1975 by Tom and Carole Dehlinger, the winery has remained dedicated to crafting small-lot, estate-grown wines that capture the character of its distinctive hillside soils and cool coastal climate. Tom Dehlinger was only 28 when he planted the first 14 acres of vines on what had been an old apple ranch near Vine Hill Road. At the time, the Russian River Valley appellation was not yet nationally recognized, and winegrowing infrastructure was sparse. With degrees in biochemistry and studies in viticulture and enology, Dehlinger combined scientific rigor with a hands-on pioneer spirit, planting classic varieties such as Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Cabernet Sauvignon, and Syrah. Twenty years ago a wine friend of mine served me Dehlinger Pinot Noir from the High Plains Vineyard. I was enchanted by the Burgundian-like complexity and the supple power and grace of the wine. When I called up to try to buy some, I was told all their wines were sold to their waiting list. When I tried to get on the waiting list to buy some, I was told there was a waiting list to get on the waiting list. On my recent visit I was happy to find that, while scarce, it is now considerably easier to buy their wine. Over the decades the estate grew to roughly 45 acres of vineyards, and the family learned how different soils — from the sandy Goldridge to the denser Altamont soils — shaped the character of the fruit. Today, wines are often labeled not just by varietal but by site-specific expression, such as Goldridge and Altamont Pinot Noirs, reflecting the subtle influences of soil and sun on flavor. Dehlinger remains independent and family-run, with Tom and Carole’s daughters, Carmen and Eva Dehlinger, at the helm of 4101 Vine Hill Road, Sebastopol, CA 95472 707 823-2378 tastings by appointment Eva Dehlinger is in charge of winemaking and viticulture.

articles.text: This past week a Piedmont resident spotted a large great horned owl on the branch of a redwood tree on their property. The bird grew increasingly irritated as the residents drew closer to the base of the tree. The Post spoke with a representative from Lindsay Wildlife Experience to understand if there was reason to be concerned and to learn how to co-exist with the bird. “It is possible that the owl is resting during the day, and it feels that people are getting too close. If that’s the case, the bird will eventually move on. If it stays, it may be defending a nest,” said Peter Flowers, Wildlife Hospital and Rehabilitation Manager. Nesting season for the great horned owl is generally January through March. The total nesting period can last 4 to 5 weeks of incubation and 5 to 7 weeks until fledging of the young. They will use the nests of other raptors rather than building their own. Sometimes you can see their nest high up in the tree. Otherwise, you have to depend upon their defending the area as an indication. They will also hoot nightly to indicate their territory to other birds. “Great Horned owls are territorial but generally not a threat to people unless defending a nest, in which case they may hiss, raise their wings, clack their beak, but rarely dive at you,” said Flowers. Photo courtesy of Lindsay Wildlife Museum A great horned owl “If an owl is nesting nearby, it is best not to approach. Do not make eye contact, keep noise to a minimum, and keep pets away. Smaller pets should stay inside and be outside on leash or supervised,” Flowers said. Flowers advises residents who see an owl in their neighborhood to avoid using rodenticides, consider window decals to prevent potential window strikes, and remove hazards such as netting or fishing line. When not nesting, the great horned owl will patrol its normal territory and find its favorite spots to stop and rest. If there is a great horned owl in your neighborhood, it can be quite beneficial in keeping the rodent population under control. If residents want to learn more about local raptors, veteran raptor biologist Allen Fish will discuss the raptors living in the East Bay and share stories of high-speed chases, family drama, and near miraculous survivals. His talk will be at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Wednesday, March 11 at 6:30 p.m.

Piedmont owl sighting leads to advice on urban wildlife By Jake Lannon This past week a Piedmont resident spotted a large great horned owl on the branch of a redwood tree on their property. The bird grew increasingly irritated as the residents drew closer to the base of the tree. The Post spoke with a representative from Lindsay Wildlife Experience to understand if there was reason to be concerned and to learn how to co-exist with the bird. “It is possible that the owl is resting during the day, and it feels that people are getting too close. If that’s the case, the bird will eventually move on. If it stays, it may be defending a nest,” said Peter Flowers, Wildlife Hospital and Rehabilitation Manager. Nesting season for the great horned owl is generally January through March. The total nesting period can last 4 to 5 weeks of incubation and 5 to 7 weeks until fledging of the young. They will use the nests of other raptors rather than building their own. Sometimes you can see their nest high up in the tree. Otherwise, you have to depend upon their defending the area as an indication. They will also hoot nightly to indicate their territory to other birds. “Great Horned owls are territorial but generally not a threat to people unless defending a nest, in which case they may hiss, raise their wings, clack their beak, but rarely dive at you,” said Flowers. Photo courtesy of Lindsay Wildlife Museum A great horned owl “If an owl is nesting nearby, it is best not to approach. Do not make eye contact, keep noise to a minimum, and keep pets away. Smaller pets should stay inside and be outside on leash or supervised,” Flowers said. Flowers advises residents who see an owl in their neighborhood to avoid using rodenticides, consider window decals to prevent potential window strikes, and remove hazards such as netting or fishing line. When not nesting, the great horned owl will patrol its normal territory and find its favorite spots to stop and rest. If there is a great horned owl in your neighborhood, it can be quite beneficial in keeping the rodent population under control.
